prompt.context:
Ecosystems International (EI) is a nonprofit organization that works to preserve endangered ecosystems throughout the world. The organization is comprised of a headquarters and 120 local offices across the globe. Historically, headquarters has provided local offices with standardized curriculum and marketing materials, but each local office has operated independently with its own board of directors, operating processes, and data management systems. In recent years, EI headquarters has been working to change this, particularly in regards to data management. In order to better fundraise with corporate-level donors, EI headquarters wants to be able to see and report real-time information on the organization's volunteers and fundraising information. EI recently mandated that local offices convert to a central CRM over the next five years. This mandate was met with great resistance from many local offices and since the beginning of the project, headquarters has been concerned about the success and reputation of the project.

Using an internal team, EI piloted implementing the CRM system at six local offices. Each of these offices had different legacy data management systems and business process transformations that needed to be taken into consideration. After a year of piloting the system, the project has suffered considerable challenges. EI headquarters is receiving calls from local office leadership complaining that the system is cumbersome and employees are tremendously overworked trying to adjust to it. In addition, the implementation team is struggling because each local office's data varies greatly, local office leadership is not engaging their staff to adapt to the new system, and there is considerable evidence that employees are not actually using the system.

Overall, the local office pilots have not been successful and word is spreading throughout the entire organization that the CRM adoption is a colossal failure. EI has brought you in to advise them on next steps.
prompt.question: The team would like help determining: (1) Who are the stakeholders that need to be most considered in order to achieve success? (2) What risks does EI face in this project? (3) What approach should EI take to ensure that this project does not fail? How should it implement the software for the other 114 locations?

clarifying_info.a: The organization is comprised of a headquarters and 120 local offices. Local offices vary greatly in structure and size, ranging from 1–100 employees. Some are flat; others have multiple branches and hierarchies. No two local offices are structured the same.

Globally, EI has a highly independent culture. Employees are resilient, if not slightly stubborn. Many offices resist change initiated by headquarters. Local offices have the right to manage much of their business independently and each has elements of its own unique culture. Local offices can operate in different languages and are composed of diverse sets of employees.

clarifying_info.q: Why is this change taking place? What are the main objectives?
clarifying_info.a: HQ would like a better data management system to aid in its fundraising goals. EI headquarters also (unpublicly) believes changing to this CRM will improve operational efficiencies in the local offices.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a timeline for when the implementation needs to be complete?
clarifying_info.a: EI HQ was hoping to have all 120 local offices using the system within the next five years.

clarifying_info.q: Has EI ever done anything like this before?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. EI attempted to switch to a different CRM five years ago and failed—the software could not handle the amount of data EI wanted to store, resulting in extremely long wait times. After two years, HQ abandoned the project. This failed implementation caused the 120 local offices to distrust headquarters and its ability to implement software systems, and HQ lost a considerable amount of money.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current skill set of the implementation team?
clarifying_info.a: The headquarters employees on the implementation team are well qualified to conduct software implementations, but they lack manpower due to budget constraints and there is not enough money to hire more team members.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the end users of the CRM?
clarifying_info.a: The end users will be the local office employees. Most local office employees do not have training in the CRM system; those who do are young and not in high-level positions.

clarifying_info.q: Are there change champions for the project?
clarifying_info.a: EI has not yet established change champions, but this is a good consideration.

clarifying_info.q: What learnings did the implementation team take from the pilot phase?
clarifying_info.a: (1) Data varies greatly from office to office—local offices currently maintain data in different systems such as Excel, Access, and other localized CRM systems, making uniform legacy data conversion difficult. (2) Leadership in three of the six pilot sites has outwardly expressed disdain for the new system to HQ, their own employees, and other office leadership. (3) Training was unsuccessful—a uniform training approach did not adjust for each office's different operational processes and data priorities, and bugs in the system meant it did not function as the trainings demonstrated. (4) Many employees are still using old Excel or Access documents and not actively entering data into the new CRM.

framework: Stakeholder identification: map key stakeholders at HQ, local office leadership, and end-user employee levels; assess their influence and current disposition toward the project
Risk assessment: identify project risks across people (resistance, leadership misalignment), process (data heterogeneity, training gaps), and technology (system bugs, adoption failure) dimensions
Change management approach: develop a structured plan covering leadership alignment, communications, incentives, change champions, and tailored training
Implementation sequencing: leverage pilot learnings to sequence remaining 114 offices, starting with willing/aligned offices and building momentum
Measurement and contingency: define success metrics and milestones throughout the rollout; establish contingency plans if adoption falters

questions.prompt: Who are the key stakeholders and what are their primary concerns?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify at least three tiers: (1) EI HQ leadership—want successful CRM adoption to enable real-time fundraising data and operational efficiencies; (2) Local office leadership—concerned about disruption, workload, loss of autonomy, and credibility given prior failed CRM attempt; (3) Local office employees (end users)—concerned about learning curve, productivity loss, and system reliability. Excellent candidates note that corporate donors are an indirect stakeholder because the whole initiative was motivated by their reporting needs, and that the organization's prior CRM failure heightens skepticism at all levels.

questions.prompt: What are the major risks EI faces in this project?
questions.guidance: Key risks include: (1) Reputational risk—word is already spreading that the implementation is a failure, which could undermine all 120 offices before rollout begins; (2) Leadership resistance—three of six pilot leaders have actively undermined the project; (3) Low adoption—employees are continuing to use legacy systems, meaning the data will be incomplete and inaccurate; (4) Data heterogeneity—different source systems (Excel, Access, localized CRMs) make data migration inconsistent; (5) Capacity constraint—the implementation team lacks sufficient manpower; (6) Training gaps—one-size-fits-all training failed to account for different office processes and system bugs; (7) Trust deficit from prior failed CRM project—HQ has limited credibility on software implementations.

questions.prompt: What approach should EI take for the remaining 114 locations? Walk through your recommendation.
questions.guidance: A strong recommendation covers all five areas: (1) Leadership Alignment—survey leaders to identify allies; start implementations with offices led by supportive leaders; have positive leaders speak to resistant ones; communicate benefits and leadership's role explicitly; (2) Communications—tailor messaging by stakeholder group; cascade communications from local office leadership downward; be transparent about learning curve and short-term productivity impact; (3) Incentives—create visible recognition and awards for offices/teams that move the project forward; celebrate milestones; (4) Stakeholder Engagement / Change Champions—identify change champions who are positive and understand the business at each office; use them to gather feedback and drive adoption; account for language and cultural differences; (5) Training—redesign training to address specific business needs and operational processes of each local office rather than using a uniform approach. Excellent candidates also propose measuring success (e.g., CRM data completeness, user login rates, leadership survey scores) and outline contingency plans if adoption continues to lag.

brainstorming.prompt: What methods could EI use to increase employee adoption of the new CRM at local offices?

categories.name: Leadership & Culture
ideas: Identify and empower change champions at each local office
Require local office leaders to visibly use and endorse the system
Pair resistant offices with enthusiastic peer leaders for mentoring
Recognize offices publicly when they hit adoption milestones

categories.name: Training & Support
ideas: Redesign training to reflect each office's specific data and operational workflows
Offer role-based training tracks rather than one-size-fits-all sessions
Provide on-site support staff during go-live periods
Create a help desk or peer support network for ongoing questions
Develop quick-reference job aids in local languages

categories.name: Communications
ideas: Send targeted communications that articulate benefits for each stakeholder group
Use local office leadership as the messenger rather than HQ
Set clear expectations about temporary productivity loss during transition
Share success stories from pilot offices that are going well

categories.name: Incentives & Recognition
ideas: Award offices or teams with highest adoption rates
Gamify data entry completeness with leaderboards
Tie leadership performance reviews to successful CRM adoption in their offices
Celebrate milestone completions organization-wide

categories.name: Implementation Process
ideas: Sequence rollout starting with the most willing and aligned offices
Use learnings from each prior conversion to improve the next
Standardize data migration playbooks while allowing local customization
Pilot a revised approach with a seventh, more cooperative office before broad rollout
Allocate additional capacity by temporarily redeploying internal staff or phasing rollout more slowly

recommendation: EI should pause the broad rollout and conduct a structured reset before proceeding to the remaining 114 offices
Immediately address the reputational damage by communicating transparently with all local office leadership about what went wrong in the pilots and what will change
Re-sequence the rollout to start with offices led by supportive leaders, using their successes to rebuild organizational trust
Rebuild the implementation approach around five pillars: leadership alignment, tailored communications, incentives, change champions, and office-specific training
risks: Continued rollout without changes risks further erosion of trust and near-certain adoption failure across all 120 offices
Budget constraints limit the ability to expand the implementation team, so capacity must be managed carefully through phasing
Remaining time in the five-year mandate is limited; a slow reset must be balanced against the deadline
If the CRM system itself has unresolved bugs, no change management effort will produce adoption—HQ must confirm the technology is stable before re-engaging offices
next_steps: Survey all local office leadership to assess disposition and identify change champions
Resolve known system bugs with the CRM vendor
Redesign training curricula for the next wave of offices based on their specific processes
Establish a communications plan and milestone measurement framework before the next office goes live
Define success metrics (e.g., weekly active users, data completeness rate) to track adoption rigorously
